tests.description: Timed check on The Biological Approach

questions.question: Describe the key assumptions of the biological approach and explain how genes influence behaviour.
questions.correctAnswer: The biological approach assumes behaviour is caused by biological processes: genes (inherited predispositions), neurochemistry (neurotransmitter activity), brain structure (localised functions), and evolution (naturally selected behaviours). Genes influence behaviour through heredity - twin studies show higher MZ than DZ concordance for many traits, suggesting genetic influence.

questions.question: Evaluate the biological approach, considering its strengths and limitations.
questions.correctAnswer: Strengths: scientific (uses objective methods like brain scanning, drug trials, twin studies), practical applications (drug treatments based on neurochemistry), has predictive power (identifies risk factors). Limitations: reductionist (reduces complex behaviour to genes and chemicals), deterministic (implies free will is an illusion), ignores environmental influences (cannot explain why MZ twins d

questions.question: Discuss whether behaviour is determined by biology, referring to the nature-nurture debate.
questions.correctAnswer: Nature argument: behaviour is determined by biology (genes, brain, neurochemistry). Supported by: twin studies, evolution, brain damage case studies. Nurture argument: behaviour is shaped by experience. Supported by: cultural differences, learning theory, plasticity. Conclusion: both contribute - the diathesis-stress model shows genetic vulnerability interacts with environmental triggers. Neither

questions.correctAnswer: A grade 9 response will: outline key assumptions (genes, neurochemistry, brain structure, evolution); present supporting evidence (twin studies, brain scanning, drug effectiveness); evaluate strengths (scientific, practical applications, testable); evaluate limitations (reductionist, deterministic, ignores environment, cannot explain MZ twin differences); consider the interactionist alternative (diathesis-stress, biopsychosocial); conclude: the biological approach provides valuable scientific insights and effective treatments but is incomplete alone - behaviour is best understood through the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors.
